income_forms.fit: You walk into a client's situation and within a short conversation you have located the gap: a supplier charging too much, a process that duplicates effort, a contact who needs exactly what another party is discarding. You do not wait for a formal brief. You propose the trade, name the decision, and sketch the next step before the meeting ends. The client pays for your read of the room and your ability to move resources toward the opening, not for a credential on the wall. This matches the chart's dominant Wealth family and the light Direct Resource, which means you rarely wait for permission or formal backing before acting.
income_forms.friction: The friction is that you open new fronts faster than you consolidate. A consulting engagement ends, you bank the fee, and you are already scanning for the next opening before you have written down what the last one actually returned or whether any part of it could run without you. The chart has no Companion and no Output, so there is no built-in counterweight that slows the opportunistic instinct down or forces you to document what worked. Without a consolidation checkpoint, you leave repeatable arrangements on the table and start each engagement from zero.

leaks.how_it_shows: You work best with a small number of people who can move quickly and do not require consensus. But the chart has no Companion, so you do not naturally build peer structures that share ownership and report back. In practice, you either do everything yourself or you bring in a collaborator and then outrun them — you open the next front before the first has been consolidated, and the collaborator is left holding a piece that no longer fits the move. The leak is not the partnership itself; it is that you do not build the reporting rhythm that would let a partner own a piece and feed it back to you.
leaks.rule: If you are about to bring in a collaborator on a new opening, then first write down what the last opening returned and whether it is still running without you; if you cannot answer both in one sentence, do not sign the collaborator yet.

conservative.description: Build the steady base first and let the opportunistic stream feed it. The chart's Direct Wealth is the heaviest single weight, so the base is not optional — it is the point. In practice: keep a fixed monthly arrangement that covers your floor, route a set share of every opportunistic win into that arrangement before you touch the rest, and cap the number of open fronts at one at a time until the base holds. The luck pillar starting around age 43 brings water and earth more strongly, giving the steady-building side more room to hold, so this strategy fits best from that point onward.
conservative.preconditions: You need a floor income that does not depend on the next opening, and you need a written consolidation checkpoint that you actually use. Without the checkpoint, the conservative strategy collapses into the same leak as the aggressive one. The chart has no Companion and no Output, so the checkpoint has to be external — a fixed slot, a person who asks, a format you cannot skip.

balanced.description: Run a mixed rhythm: a steady base from repeatable arrangements plus a faster stream from opportunistic moves, with a mandatory consolidation slot between them. The chart supports this because Direct Wealth and Indirect Wealth are the joint heaviest family, so the steady base and the opportunistic engine are both real. The luck pillar starting around age 43 supports routing part of every opportunistic win into the steady base.
balanced.preconditions: You need a time structure with short cycles and low formal barriers, and you need collaborators who can own a piece and report back without demanding consensus. The chart has no Companion, so peer-heavy consensus environments drain you; the balanced strategy requires a small number of fast-moving collaborators, not a committee. You also need the consolidation slot to be fixed, not optional.
